items.question: What strikes you about the diversity of robot embodiments in the RTX datasets?

items.answer: The data sets that resulted, even starting from those criteria, were so diverse. items.question: How do you explain the acceleration of robotics research in the era of internet-scale foundation models?
items.object: The acceleration of robotics research through internet-scale foundation models
items.answer: Definitely the feeling that we're living through an inflection point right now. I think, as Kira said, a year ago between GPT-2 and GPT-3, and maybe nowadays it's closer to the era of GPT-3 time in robotics. I think it's definitely been pretty top of mind for me. To think about why that happens is kind of interesting. My one sentence explanation is that with the era of internet scale foundation models, things that used to work maybe 20 or 30% of the time are now working 60 to 70% of the time. In robotics, it's a very complicated, dynamic engineered system with many pieces. In the past, if every small component of your entire system only worked 30% of the time, it would take many iterations to get a whole performance system working at scale. But now, when every single part of the entire stack just works that much better, from the research iteration process to the engineering scaling process to the data collection engines, I think you can really see the pace increase when you have many more successes and a much higher hit rate when scaling up your research. That's my one sentence explanation.

items.question: How do you think about RT-2's approach to connecting robot-specific data with internet knowledge?
items.object: RT-2 as a bridge between robot-specific data and internet knowledge
items.answer:
I think the framing I really like to think about this is, in all of the works we'll be discussing today, and especially RT-2, we're bridging the gap between robot-specific data with their custom input spaces and custom objects and physical reasoning and custom action representations and outputs, and internet data and internet concepts, which have been sitting in this whole other pile way off. With all of these works we're trying to bridge these two worlds together to enable more transfer, to better leverage the immense amounts of reasoning and capabilities already contained in internet data. We're trying to make robotics more similar to that, and bring together concepts on the internet and bring them to robotics.

I think RT-2, exactly as you said, is doing this by making the action outputs literally just tokens, literally just language.

items.question: How do you assess the diversity of robot embodiments in RTX given its restriction to single-arm manipulators with two-fingered grippers and a single camera view?
items.answer: This seems like a very limiting assumption, but even then you can see that the datasets that resulted were so diverse. We have everything from pick and place with small WidowX robots using baby toys, all the way to industrial arms, big beefy ones, to the mobile manipulator we have at Google, all the way to very dexterous cable routing robots from Berkeley. Even with this very limiting assumption, you still get so many different morphologies.

items.question: How do you think about whether future robots will converge on a single morphology, such as a humanoid?
items.object: Specialization versus a single general-purpose robot morphology
items.answer: For me, it's an open question. I see a lot of benefits of specialization. We have specialized robots in every household today; they're called refrigerators, toasters, microwaves, and dishwashers. You don't have one single kind of robot that does it all at an average level. I do think there are arguments that we will continue to see specialization.
quotes: Will we just have one single morphology, maybe a humanoid, or many different ones? For me, it's an open question. I see a lot of benefits of specialization. I do think there are arguments that we will continue to see specialization.

items.question: What do you see as the most impactful result of releasing RTX for robotics research?
items.object: RTX's impact on cross-embodiment robotics research
items.answer: Building on Kira's point, the release of RTX is not really just about the model itself, not just the fact that we can train one model with them all. This is the starting line, not the finish line. This is a new chapter of robotics research. By nature, you can now start by default assuming you're in the multi-robot, cross-embodiment regime. We haven't necessarily seen a ton of work that takes the literal checkpoint we released and fine-tunes on top of that. By definition, academic labs like to search for new problems with new model decisions. But we have seen many projects building off the released dataset and data pipelines that we also open-sourced with the RTX paper, and I think that has really been very impactful. For example, a work from Berkeley recently called Octo has their own generalist policy checkpoint that trains across many different robots. They have some new design decisions, like adding diffusion heads, but they also assume by default that they're in this cross-embodiment, multi-robot setting, where they train and evaluate on many different robots. To me, that's the most impactful result of RTX: people are now excited about cross-embodiment research, and it's now possible with the datasets and data infrastructure that came with RTX.

items.question: What do you think PIVOT reveals about the physical knowledge already contained in pretrained vision-language models?
items.object: PIVOT and the physical knowledge in pretrained vision-language models
items.answer:
I empathize with your view that this is kind of an odd one out in the works we discuss today. Those are really about building, fine-tuning end-to-end models, training them for robotics tasks on a lot of data, and scaling them up in the real world. In PIVOT, I view this more as a result that was so exciting about a trend we found that we didn't know if other folks in the community were thinking about. We wanted to share that these pretrained internet-scale VLMs can understand some notions of motion, causality, robot trajectories, and contact.

This was a bit surprising, because in a lot of our team's perception, and to be honest most of the community right now in both language modeling and robotics, it's like, “Of course, there are so many things in robotics that we have to tackle ourselves. The dense contact spatial reasoning—left, right, up, down—these are concepts that aren't contained in Wikipedia, Reddit, or image generation datasets. These are things we need hardcore robotics data for.” Perhaps recently, with this work, the answer is that there is already a good amount of physical intelligence contained in internet-trained models by themselves, without any robot data pretraining or fine-tuning. I don't think internet data alone, just watching Reddit threads and Wikipedia, is enough to solve contact-rich robotics. But I do think we've so far just been seeing the tip of the iceberg for the knowledge already contained in these large VLMs.

With PIVOT, by showing that if you have this external prior, this inductive bias of a robust optimization problem, and make it very easy for the VLM to pick and choose in a multiple-choice setting which direction the robot should go, and run multiple iterations, we show that you can better drag out the implicit knowledge contained in these VLMs. I don't think the results mean you can take PIVOT, apply it to any robot, and it'll work off the shelf. The performance is very far away from RT-2 or any fine-tuned policy. But the fact that it shows promising signs of life was unexpected, and I hope is inspiring to others.

items.question: How do you assess the gap between today's robotics capabilities and the full vision of embodied AGI?
items.object: Robotics’ readiness for commercial use and embodied AGI
items.answer: I agree 100% that we're a few breakthroughs away from general purpose robotics, the dream we're all working so hard for. If you want something commercially viable, something that will maybe make money or help some people in the world, I think a lot of those ingredients are already ready to have a larger impact than maybe even just a few short months or years ago. But for the true full vision of embodied AGI, I do think there are still fundamentally a few open research challenges.
